claims.text: Successful homogeneous formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by synchronization of metal-precursor reduction kinetics.
Simultaneous precursor reduction causes nucleation events for the constituent metals to overlap.
Overlapping reduction and nucleation yield a uniform, single-phase alloy.
Unsynchronized reduction causes sequential nucleation and phase segregation.
The intended starting material contains five or more noble metal species in soluble form.
A tailored thermal ramp and mixing order can force the reductions of all metal types to overlap.
Moderate-temperature reduction of a solid, mixed precursor limits free-atom mobility.
Uniform elemental dispersion without core-shell or phase-separated regions indicates a homogeneous nanoparticle.
Reduction synchrony favors random incorporation of different metals into nascent nuclei before atomic mobility can induce segregation.
Early-reduced metals act as seeds that bias later deposition and thereby produce elemental segregation or phase separation.
The synchronized treatment will produce nanoparticles with more uniform composition, homogeneous lattice structures, and evenly dispersed noble metal atoms.
The unsynchronized baseline will produce more phase-separated or core-shell regions because of disparate reduction timing.
The proposed synchronization mechanism applies to solution-based or low-temperature single-source precursor reductions with limited atom mobility.
The proposed synchronization mechanism may not apply to carbothermal-shock or microwave syntheses because extreme thermal conditions dominate kinetics and mixing.
The effect of synchronization on homogeneity may vary with precursor chemistry and processing details.
Stochastic nanoparticle nucleation may produce variability even under synchronized conditions.
A controlled comparison can isolate the effect of enforcing reduction synchrony by holding the reaction environment otherwise constant.
Failure of the synchronized protocol to produce a statistically significant improvement in homogeneity over the unsynchronized baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The central fields claim that synchronized reduction governs single-phase HEA formation and that consecutive reduction causes segregation, but cited record PMC10621632::web::027::conclusions reports that five-element single-phase HEA particles formed even when the elements reduced consecutively. That record instead attributes alloying to the number of atom types and limited mobility.
